title: IDF Rarity Scoring — Core Method
description: Inverse document frequency turns rarity into a number: a term appearing in few documents gets a high IDF, and a record's rarity score is the sum of its terms' IDFs. Sorting by this score surfaces the records built from the archive's most unusual vocabulary — exactly the ones ordinary relevance ranking buries. The formula needs only document frequencies, so it runs over any indexed collection without training. Search engineers have used IDF since the 1970s; here it is repurposed from ranking matches to hunting obscurity. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Tail-Term Mining — Core Method
description: Every archive has a vocabulary tail: terms that appear once or twice across millions of records. Tail-term mining scans the term dictionary for these singletons and doubletons, then lists the records containing them — the natural habitat of obscure information. Because the tail is huge, the miner samples and estimates rather than enumerating everything. The output is a watchlist of terms no ordinary query would ever include, each pointing at records almost nobody has read. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
from collections import Counter
corpus = ["archive deep search", "archive index", "zephyr archive",
          "archive deep search", "quixotic index"]
cnt = Counter(w for doc in corpus for w in doc.split())
tail = [w for w, c in cnt.items() if c == 1]
print("tail terms:", tail)
for w in tail:
    hits = [d for d in corpus if w in d.split()]
    print(" %r appears in %d record(s)" % (w, len(hits)))

title: Outlier Detection — Core Method
description: Rarity is not only about words: records with extreme numeric features — the longest document, the oldest timestamp, the highest citation count — are found with z-scores. Any record more than a few standard deviations from the mean on a feature is flagged as an outlier worth inspecting. Combining z-scores across several features with a max or sum catches records that are unusual in any dimension. This statistical lens finds the archive's oddballs without any vocabulary at all. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Low-Coverage Query Expansion — Core Method
description: Ordinary queries use common words and therefore return common records; the rare-record finder deliberately expands queries toward low-coverage vocabulary. Given a seed term, it looks up co-occurring rare terms in the collection statistics and adds the rarest ones to the query. Each expansion step is logged so the user sees exactly which obscure terms were introduced. This inverts the usual goal of query expansion — instead of improving recall of the obvious, it steers the search into the archive's neglected corners. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — public methods from established computer-science practice.

title: Rarity-Ranked Sampling — Core Method
description: When the archive is too large to scan fully, rarity-ranked sampling draws a small subset biased toward unusual records instead of a uniform random sample. Each record's selection probability is proportional to its rarity score, so a thousand-record sample can contain more obscurity than a million-record uniform draw. The sampler is deterministic given a seed, which makes rare-record surveys reproducible. This is how auditors and researchers survey the long tail without reading the whole archive. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import random
random.seed(7)
recs = [("d%d" % i, 1.0 / (i + 1)) for i in range(20)]
total = sum(r for _, r in recs)
sample = []
for _ in range(5):
    x = random.random() * total
    for name, r in recs:
        x -= r
        if x <= 0:
            sample.append(name); break
print("rarity-biased sample:", sample)
